content.title: Artemis II recap: Live updates from astronauts flying around far side of moon
content.text: 9:35 pm ET April 6, 2026Artemis II lunar flyby science observations are winding downRick NealeAfter nearly seven hours, the astronauts' lunar observation period is wrapping up.8:51 pm ET April 6, 2026NASA releases video of Artemis II spacecraft as solar eclipse beginsRick Neale8:39 pm ET April 6, 2026Solar eclipse underway for Artemis II crew as moon passes in front of sunRick NealeSolar-eclipse information from NASA:"Artemis II is now entering a solar eclipse that will last for about an hour as Orion, the Moon and the Sun align. During this phase, the crew will see the Sun disappear behind a mostly darkened Moon," an online update said."The crew will use the opportunity to study the solar corona — the Sun’s outermost atmosphere — as it glows around the lunar edge. They also will watch for flashes of light from meteoroids striking the surface, which could offer insight into potential hazards on the Moon," the update said.8:33 pm ET April 6, 2026Artemis II astronauts end breaks, prepare to observe solar eclipseRick NealeThe Orion spacecraft is positioned so the crew can watch the upcoming solar eclipse, which should start in two minutes.8:11 pm ET April 6, 2026Artemis II solar eclipse coming up within 25 minutesRick NealeNext, the moon will pass in front of the sun at 8:35 p.m. from the crew's perspective. This solar eclipse should last until 9:32 p.m.During an afternoon briefing, Kelsey Young, Artemis science officer, reminded the astronauts to wear eclipse glasses during the event.Young also reminded the crew to configure all three onboard cameras for coronal and deep-sky observations during the eclipse.7:54 pm ET April 6, 2026Here's what Artemis II Mission Specialist Christina Koch said after blackout endedRick NealeNASA's Artemis program just shared this exchange between astronaut Christina Koch and Mission Control after the lunar communications drought ended.7:34 pm ET April 6, 2026NASA publishes summary of Artemis II lunar blackout highlightsRick NealeWhat happened while the Orion was on the far side of the moon? NASA just posted these flyby updates on the Artemis II Flight Day 6 page:7:00 p.m.: "Orion has reached its closest approach to the Moon at about 4,067 miles above the lunar surface. At this point, the spacecraft is traveling about 60,863 miles an hour relative to Earth, but only 3,139 miles an hour relative to the Moon."7:02 p.m. "The Artemis II crew has reached the mission’s maximum distance from Earth at 252,756 miles, setting a new record for human spaceflight. This milestone places the crew 4,111 miles farther from Earth than the Apollo 13 mission in 1970." 7:24 p.m.: "The Artemis II crew witnessed an Earthrise as Orion emerged from behind the Moon, moments before the Deep Space Network reacquired the spacecraft’s signal and restored communications."7:25 pm ET April 6, 2026Communications resume between Artemis II astronauts and Mission Control in HoustonRick NealeThe planned 40-minute communications blackout has ended. The Orion spacecraft has emerged from the far side of the moon and reconnected with the Deep Space Network.7:11 pm ET April 6, 2026NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman: 'This is how we push the frontier forward'Rick NealeNASA Administrator Jared Isaacman shared the following message via tweet during the Artemis II loss-of-communications period:"A milestone for Artemis II. For the first time in more than half a century, humans are laying eyes on this side of the Moon again. Artemis II’s trajectory will also reveal parts of the Moon no human has ever seen before. This is how we push the frontier forward," Isaacman said.7:03 pm ET April 6, 2026How far did the Orion spacecraft venture from Earth? Stay tuned.Rick NealeAt 7:02 p.m., NASA officials expected Orion to reach its maximum distance from Earth at 252,756 miles. This distance is unprecedented in history.Exact numbers will be released later.6:58 pm ET April 6, 2026Artemis II astronauts expected to make closest approach to moon's surfaceRick NealeNASA's communications blackout remains ongoing, as the Orion spacecraft is still beyond the far side of the moon.But NASA officials expect the Orion to make its closest approach to the moon at 7 p.m., traveling within 4,067 miles of the lunar surface.6:44 pm ET April 6, 2026Lunar blackout begins: Moon blocks communications between Orion and EarthRick NealeNASA officials just announced that the Artemis II roughly 40-minute communications blackout has begun.During the blackout, the Orion should make its closest approach to the moon's surface at 7 p.m., passing within 4,066 miles.Then at 7:02 p.m., the crew should set a new deep-space record by reaching a maximum distance from Earth of 252,755 miles. 6:24 pm ET April 6, 2026Artemis II astronauts now about 20 minutes away from losing communicationsRick NealeNASA officials estimate the Orion spacecraft will swing around the far side of the moon about 6:41 p.m. to 6:44 p.m. — blocking communications with Earth via the Deep Space Network.The lunar blackout should last roughly 40 minutes.6:15 pm ET April 6, 2026See the video of Artemis II crew suggesting to name crater for commander's late wifeRick NealeWatch the astronauts' reactions earlier this afternoon when they provisionally named a moon crater in honor of commander Reid Wiseman’s late wife, Carroll Taylor Wiseman.She died in 2020 after a five-year battle with cancer.5:56 pm ET April 6, 2026Artemis II lunar flyby images captured in photo galleryRick NealeCheck out this USA Today Network photo gallery featuring images of the ongoing Artemis II lunar flyby.5:34 pm ET April 6, 2026Artemis II astronauts to splash down Friday night in Pacific OceanRick NealeThe Artemis II astronauts' Orion spacecraft is scheduled to splash down off the coast of San Diego, California, at about 8:07 p.m. EST Friday, April 10."Following splashdown, recovery teams will retrieve the crew members using helicopters and deliver them to the USS John P. Murtha. Once aboard, the astronauts will undergo post-flight medical evaluations in the ship’s medical bay before traveling back to shore to meet with an aircraft bound for NASA Johnson (Space Center)," a NASA press release said.5:21 pm ET April 6, 2026NASA-SpaceX ISS supply launch moves to Thursday from Cape CanaveralRick NealeNASA's SpaceX NG-24 launch has moved back from Wednesday morning to Thursday morning from Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station.The SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket will launch a Northrop Grumman Cygnus XL spacecraft carrying NASA science investigations, supplies and equipment up to the International Space Station. More information:Launch: 8:26 a.m. Thursday, April 9.Trajectory: Northeast.Central Florida sonic booms: Yes.Live FLORIDA TODAY Space Team coverage: Starts 90 minutes before liftoff at floridatoday.com/space.4:49 pm ET April 6, 2026NASA press release hails Artemis II eclipsing record for farthest crewed spaceflightRick NealeA NASA afternoon press release highlighted comments from space by Artemis II mission specialist Jeremy Hansen:"From the cabin of Integrity here, as we surpass the furthest distance humans have ever traveled from planet Earth, we do so in honoring the extraordinary efforts and feats of our predecessors in human space exploration," Hansen said."We will continue our journey even further into space before Mother Earth succeeds in pulling us back to everything that we hold dear. But we most importantly choose this moment to challenge this generation and the next to make sure this record is not long-lived," he said.4:34 pm ET April 6, 2026NASA announces refined times of upcoming lunar flyby milestonesRick Neale6:41 p.m.: Loss of communications for about 40 minutes as the crew heads behind the moon.7 p.m.: The Orion spacecraft makes its closest approach to the moon's surface at 4,066 miles.7:02 p.m.: Orion reaches its maximum distance from Earth at 252,755 miles. 7:21 p.m.: Crew reemerges from behind the moon and sees an “Earthrise” as our planet returns to view, and then communications resume a few minutes later.4:17 pm ET April 6, 2026Read more about Artemis II proposal to name crater for commander's late wifeRick NealeFLORIDA TODAY Space Reporter Brooke Edwards wrote this story about the crew provisionally naming a moon crater in honor of commander Reid Wiseman’s late wife, Carroll Taylor Wiseman, earlier this afternoon."After this mission is complete, the crater name proposals will be formally submitted to the International Astronomical Union, the organization that governs the naming of celestial bodies and their surface features," a NASA online update said.3:59 pm ET April 6, 2026Mission Control: Orion's troublesome toilet is 'no-go for use'Rick NealeIn a vehicle system update, the Artemis II astronauts were just informed that "the toilet right now is no-go for use."Rather, the crew should use CCUs, or collapsible contingency urinals, said Jenni Gibbons, a Canadian Space Agency astronaut and Artemis backup astronaut working at Mission Control in Houston.3:43 pm ET April 6, 2026Check out this US Geological Survey rotating map of the moon's surfaceRick NealeRetired Canadian astronaut Chris Hadfield, who flew two NASA space shuttle missions and logged a long-duration stay on the International Space Station, shared this U.S. Geological Survey rotating moon-map animation in a tweet."A timely map to have as a reference as the Artemis crew skims past the Moon today, taking new hi-res & low-light photos," Hadfield said.3:25 pm ET April 6, 2026Artemis II astronauts describing lunar geographic features to Mission ControlRick NealeKelsey Young, Artemis science officer, is chatting with crew members as they describe what they're viewing outside the windows of their Orion spacecraft.3:07 pm ET April 6, 2026Artemis II Orion spacecraft is now less than 10,000 miles from the moonRick NealeAs a reminder, the spacecraft will make its closest approach to the moon at 7:02 p.m. That's when the Orion will pass 4,070 miles above the lunar surface.2:50 pm ET April 6, 2026Astronauts begin flyby; moon observations to continue through 9:20 p.m.Rick NealeCrew members are now observing the moon through the windows of their Orion spacecraft — and they say they can see both the moon and Earth at the same time.NASA defines the nearly seven-hour Artemis II lunar observation period as "the duration of time that the crew is close enough to the Moon to make impactful science observations (4,070 miles altitude at closest approach) and the spacecraft is oriented such that the windows are pointed at the Moon."2:44 pm ET April 6, 2026Artemis II crew proposes to name two 'relatively fresh' moon cratersRick NealeThe Artemis II astronauts have proposed naming two lunar craters in honor of Integrity, their Orion spacecraft, and Carroll Taylor Wiseman, commander Reid Wiseman's late wife. She died in 2020 after a five-year battle with cancer.2:34 pm ET April 6, 2026NASA sets 'lunar surface targets' for crew to observe during moon flybyRick NealeIn a Flight Day 6 update, NASA officials supplied more information on the crew's upcoming science objectives:"On April 5, the science team sent the crew the final list of 30 lunar surface targets, including the Orientale basin, a nearly 600-mile-wide crater that straddles the Moon’s near and far sides. This 3.8-billion-year-old crater formed when a large object struck the lunar surface and retains clear evidence of that collision, including dramatic topography in its rings. The crew will study Orientale’s features up close and from multiple angles as they pass by," the update said."Hertzsprung basin also is on the crew’s list of targets. Northwest of Orientale, it is a nearly 400-mile-wide crater on the Moon’s far side. An older ringed basin, Hertzsprung offers a unique contrast to Orientale because its features have been degraded by subsequent impacts. By comparing the topography of the two craters, the crew’s observations will help scientists gain insight into how lunar features evolve over geologic timescales," the update said.2:12 pm ET April 6, 2026Artemis II upcoming events: Lunar flyby to begin at 2:45 p.m.Rick NealeHere's another look at the Artemis II flyby day schedule. The moon flyby should start at 2:45 p.m.2:00 pm ET April 6, 2026Artemis II crew breaks Apollo 13 record for farthest distance from EarthRick NealeAt 1:56 p.m., the Orion spacecraft traveled beyond 248,655 miles from Earth. That shattered the crewed record set by NASA's Apollo 13 on April 15, 1970.That distance will continue to increase: "The spacecraft will reach its maximum distance at 7:07 p.m., a total of 252,760 miles from Earth," a NASA blog update said.1:49 pm ET April 6, 2026Science briefing reviews details of solar eclipse, 'Earthrise' on lunar horizonRick NealeDuring a briefing with Kelsey Young, Artemis science officer, she reminded the astronauts to wear eclipse glasses during their upcoming solar eclipse.Young also reminded the crew to configure all three onboard cameras for coronal and deep-sky observations during the eclipse.During the 7:25 p.m. "Earthrise" when our planet will reappear on the moon's horizon, she said the astronauts will be looking directly at Asia, Africa and Oceania.1:36 pm ET April 6, 2026Check out NASA graphic depicting Artemis II 10-day moon missionRick NealeThis NASA graphic shows the flight path of the Orion spacecraft and its upcoming swing around the moon and back.1:23 pm ET April 6, 2026Late Apollo astronaut Jim Lovell sends greetings to Artemis II crewRick NealeAfter waking up to “Good Morning” by Mandisa and TobyMac, the astronauts listened to a recorded message from Apollo 8 and Apollo 13 astronaut Jim Lovell, who passed away in August 2025 at age 97."Hello, Artemis II. This is Apollo astronaut Jim Lovell. Welcome to my old neighborhood," Lovell said in his message recorded last year."When Frank Borman, Bill Anders, and I orbited the moon on Apollo 8, we got humanity’s first up-close look at the moon and got a view of the home planet that inspired and united people around the world. I’m proud to pass that torch on to you — as you swing around the moon and lay the groundwork for missions to Mars for the benefit of all," Lovell said."It’s a historic day, and I know how busy you’ll be. But don’t forget to enjoy the view," he said. 1:08 pm ET April 6, 2026NASA Artemis II lunar flyby streaming webcast beginsRick NealeWe've posted NASA's YouTube streaming feed above, right below the bullet-list schedule of today's key events.The Artemis II astronauts are projected to break the Apollo 13 record in 50 minutes.1:00 pm ET April 6, 2026Artemis II astronauts to receive pre-flyby briefing from NASA science officerRick NealeComing up at 1:30 p.m., a NASA science officer at Johnson Space Center in Houston will brief the Artemis crew from Mission Control on their science goals for their upcoming flyby activities.
